lessons.title: One to five — voice first
lessons.gloss: hear and say one to five before meeting their written forms

segments.text: This lesson has no Malayalam writing to decode. Hear the five words, attach each one to a quantity, and say them before your eyes meet the script.
Point to one finger and say onnŭ. Add one finger at a time: raṇṭŭ, mūnnŭ, nālŭ, añcŭ.

Malayalam and Tamil were once one language, and the family resemblance is still audible. Malayalam onnŭ sits beside Tamil onru; raṇṭŭ beside irandu; mūnnŭ beside moonru; and nālŭ beside naanku. You do not need to learn the Tamil forms. Listen only for the shared bones.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — one sound change

segments.text: Five moved furthest: an older aintu softened toward Malayalam añcŭ. Say an-chu slowly, then normally. The sound comes before its spelling.

segments.instruction: onnŭ, raṇṭŭ, mūnnŭ, nālŭ, añcŭ while raising one more finger
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *onnŭ, raṇṭŭ, mūnnŭ, nālŭ, añcŭ* while raising one more finger]

segments.instruction: say tāmasikkuka, then say jōli ceyyuka

segments.text: Count from one to five without looking. Which word means three? (Moonnu.) Which one changed furthest from its older Tamil cousin? (Anchu, five.) Next, the first three numeral shapes arrive one small step at a time.

segments.text: Say onnŭ, raṇṭŭ, mūnnŭ. You already own the meanings and sounds; this lesson adds only their three numeral shapes.
൧ means 1: onnŭ.
൨ means 2: raṇṭŭ.
൩ means 3: mūnnŭ.
Point in order, then out of order: ൩ ൧ ൨.
Keep the models visible. Finger-trace ൧, ൨, and ൩ once each. Say the number word only after your finger stops. Do not copy from memory yet.
Point to ൨ and say it. (Randu.) Which shape means three? (൩.) How many new shapes arrived? (Three.)

segments.text: Read ൧ ൨ ൩ (one, two, three). Two shapes remain in the first group.
൪ means 4: nālŭ.
൫ means 5: añcŭ.

Keep both models visible. Trace ൪ once and ൫ once. Then circle the one you hear:
Which shape means four? (൪.) Read ൫. (Anchu.) How many new shapes did this lesson add? (Two.)

segments.text: Say one to five, then read their numerals: ൧ ൨ ൩ (one, two, three) ൪ ൫ (four, five). The words themselves need only one letter you have not met.
ഒ (independent o) is independent short o. It begins ഒന്ന്, onnŭ, one.
Every other shape in this row is already familiar:
Trace ഒ (independent o) once with its model visible. Then point from ൧ to ഒന്ന് and say onnŭ. Read the remaining four rows; do not copy the whole row yet.
Which new letter begins onnŭ? (ഒ (independent o).) Read ൩ and മൂന്ന്. (Moonnu, three.) How many new letters appeared? (One.)

Copy the row once directly beneath its model. Look back after every shape if you need to. Say onnŭ through añcŭ as you check your copy. Repair only one shape.
Read ൪. (Naalu.) Which written word begins with the new letter ഒ (independent o)? (ഒന്ന്, onnŭ.) No new shape was added here.

Write the five numerals in order while the model is hidden. If one will not come, peek once, cover it again, and continue. Uncover and repair one place.
Say the row without looking. What made this harder than the previous lesson? (The model was hidden before writing.)

segments.text: Cover the answer line. You will hear familiar words, never an untaught form.
Write the three numeral shapes from sound alone. Then uncover and compare: ൨ ൫ ൩. Repair one shape if needed; do not rewrite the whole line.
Write the numeral for nālŭ from sound alone. (൪.) You are now ready to hear six through ten before meeting any of their shapes.

lessons.title: Six to ten — voice first
lessons.gloss: hear and say six to ten before meeting their written forms

segments.text: Count onnŭ through añcŭ. Keep your pencil down: the next five meanings and sounds come before their shapes.
Say the row once slowly, then once at counting speed.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — seven keeps a rare sound

segments.text: The middle sound of ēḻŭ is the curled zh heard in the name Tamil in its native form. Malayalam and Tamil kept it; Kannada and Telugu hardened it. Practise only the sound now: e-zhu. The written letter waits for a later micro-lesson.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — nine is one short of ten

segments.text: Ompathu grew from an old word for one plus pattŭ, ten: one short of ten. Before p, the older n becomes m. Say on-pattŭ slowly, then let it settle into ombatŭ.
Count six to ten. Which word preserves the rare zh? (Ezhu.) How is ombatŭ built? (One plus ten: one short of ten.) Next, the numeral shapes arrive in groups of three or fewer.

segments.text: Say āṟŭ, ēḻŭ, eṭṭŭ. Their sounds and quantities are familiar; only the shapes are new.
൬ means 6: āṟŭ.
൭ means 7: ēḻŭ.
൮ means 8: eṭṭŭ.
Point out of order: ൮ ൬ ൭.
Keep the models visible. Trace ൬, ൭, and ൮ once each. Say the word after each trace. Memory writing waits.
Which shape means seven? (൭.) Read ൮. (Ettu.) How many new shapes arrived? (Three.)

segments.text: Read ൬ ൭ ൮ (six, seven, eight). Two shapes finish the sequence.
൯ means 9: ombatŭ.
൰ means 10: pattŭ.
Point through ൬ ൭ ൮ (six, seven, eight) ൯ ൰ (nine, ten) (six to ten) and say the words once.
Trace ൯ once and ൰ once with their models visible. Circle the one you hear:
Which shape means ten? (൰.) Read ൯. (Ompathu.) This lesson added two shapes, not five.

segments.text: Say six to ten, then read ൬ ൭ ൮ (six, seven, eight) ൯ ൰ (nine, ten). Two letters remain before every written word in the row is decodable.
ഏ is independent long e.
ഴ is the curled zh you already heard in ēḻŭ.
Together with the familiar chandrakkala, they begin and finish ഏഴ്, ēḻŭ.

utterances: numeral: ൰. word: പത്ത്. said: pattŭ.

segments.text: Trace ഏ once and ഴ once with the models visible. Then point through ഏഴ് and say ēḻŭ. Whole-word memory writing waits.
Which letter carries the rare zh? (ഴ.) Read ൭ — ഏഴ്. (Ezhu, seven.) How many new letters appeared? (Two.)

Read your copied word. (Ezhu, seven.) Which numeral belongs beside it? (൭.) No new shape was added here.

segments.text: Count from onnŭ to pattŭ once without looking. No new word or shape appears in this lesson.
Read these shuffled numerals before looking back at the ordered row:
Now check against ൧ ൨ ൩ (one, two, three) ൪ ൫ (four, five) (one to five) ൬ ൭ ൮ (six, seven, eight) ൯ ൰ (nine, ten) (six to ten) (onnŭ through pattŭ).

blocks.title: Why it's said this way — meaning and history

segments.text: Which word preserves the rare zh? (ഏഴ്, ēḻŭ, seven.)
Which word means one short of ten? (ഒമ്പത്, ombatŭ, nine.)
Which first-five word shifted furthest from older aintu? (അഞ്ച്, añcŭ.)
Cover the answer.
Write its numeral and word from sound alone. Uncover and compare: ൭ — ഏഴ്. Repair one shape if needed.
Count one to ten, then read ൯ ൪ ൭ out of order. You can now hear, say, read, and write a representative part of the complete number sequence.

lessons.title: ◌് (virama) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ് — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ◌് and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ര — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
◌് (virama) — no sound of its own — it takes one away.

It is a vowel-killer. Every consonant in this script arrives with an a already inside it — that is what an abugida is. This mark takes the a back, leaving the bare consonant. It is how the script writes two consonants in a row.
You already say these, and every one of them has ◌് (virama) somewhere inside it:
നമസ്കാരം namaskāraṁ — hello / greetings (namaskāraṁ — "a making of a bow").
നന്ദി nandi — thank you.
ഇല്ല illa — no / there isn't (illa — the negative).
പേര് pēr — name.
Put your pen on ◌് (virama) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
